strengths: The paper targets an important problem: adapting large flow-matching generators from a small set of demonstrations without separately collected preference pairs. The proposed pathwise (FAIL-PD) and policy-gradient (FAIL-PG) variants cover complementary differentiable and black-box settings.

The empirical study is broad. It includes FLUX image generation, an autoregressive image model, and a video model, with evaluations of prompt following and aesthetic quality. On FLUX, the reported improvements over the base model and SFT are substantial across several automatic metrics.

The discriminator-backbone ablation, extended training curves, and experiments combining FAIL with reward optimization are useful. In particular, the observed rapid improvement followed by collapse for FAIL-PG, versus longer-term stability for FAIL-PD, is an informative practical result.

The manuscript is generally organized around clear research questions and includes task-specific learning rates, optimizer settings, evaluation sample counts, and qualitative examples. Its limitations section candidly acknowledges adversarial instability, uncertain scaling, and dependence on pretrained capabilities.
weaknesses: The central theoretical framing is not established. GAIL matches expert and policy occupancy measures over states and actions, whereas Equation 1 is an adversarial objective on final generated images—essentially conditional GAN fine-tuning. The paper does not define an imitation-learning state/action occupancy measure or prove the claimed mathematical equivalence between generative post-training and imitation learning. Consequently, claims that FAIL corrects policy drift in unseen states are not supported by the presented formulation or experiments.

FAIL-PD is described as both exact pathwise differentiation through the ODE and a single-step approximation that avoids unrolling it. Equation 2 instead trains through a locally reconstructed sample, so its gradient is generally not the exact gradient of the final-sample adversarial objective. Whether generated x0 is detached is unspecified; without detachment the claimed computational saving is unclear, while with detachment the estimator is biased. The further assertion that FAIL-PD is a low-variance, unbiased limit of DDPG with inherited local GAN convergence is given without a theorem or conditions and appears unjustified.

FAIL-PG relies on treating differences of conditional flow-matching losses as likelihood ratios and KL divergences. An ELBO is only a lower bound, and its model-dependent variational gap does not generally cancel between current and reference policies. Thus Equations 3–7 need not yield a valid probability ratio or nonnegative KL estimate. No approximation-error analysis or empirical validation against exact likelihoods is provided.

The conditional objective is underspecified. Equation 1 omits prompts, and the DINO discriminator explicitly lacks text input, so it can only match marginal image distributions and cannot directly enforce prompt-image correspondence. The hybrid-imitation update is also absent from the algorithms. Important details such as rollout group size, PPO/FPO clipping and epochs, single-step size, SFT procedure, trainable parameter subsets, discriminator feature layers and aggregation, and baseline tuning are missing.

There is a serious possible evaluation-contamination issue: training prompts are drawn from UniGen-Bench's train-en-short split, while evaluation is described as using the en-short split of 600 prompts. The manuscript does not establish that these prompt sets are disjoint. This weakens one of the headline results. Reported UniGen baselines are also inconsistent across the abstract/introduction and Tables 1 and 7, partly because different evaluators are used, making comparisons difficult to interpret.

All principal conclusions rely on automatic learned metrics, with no human evaluation despite claims about human preference, visual quality, and reward-hacking mitigation. Results have no repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests. Baselines are compared at different training horizons, and the broad discrete-image/video generalization claims are supported by only one model and one expert dataset per modality.

Originality is limited by the close relationship to ordinary adversarial generator training and prior discriminator-based diffusion training. The paper does not clearly isolate what is technically new beyond combining a GAN-style discriminator with a one-step pathwise surrogate or FPO, nor does it compare with the most relevant adversarial diffusion fine-tuning alternatives.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the claimed code/data link is blank, the expert dataset depends on a proprietary generator and incompletely specified filtering, and compute time, seeds, full baseline hyperparameters, and several algorithmic settings are absent. Presentation also needs substantial proofreading; Table 6 is visibly corrupted/overlapping, several citations appear incorrect (for example DPG-Bench is attributed to the deterministic-policy-gradient paper), and model naming is inconsistent.

The limitations discussion is welcome but incomplete. There is no research-ethics or broader-impact discussion covering licensing and provenance of synthetic and web-scraped data, generator bias, unsafe-content amplification, or the environmental cost of training on 32 H20 GPUs. Overall, the promising empirical signal does not overcome the unresolved objective/gradient validity, possible benchmark overlap, and reproducibility problems.

strengths: Originality/significance: Framing flow-model post-training as adversarial distribution matching is a useful perspective, and presenting both a differentiable pathwise variant (FAIL-PD) and a policy-gradient variant (FAIL-PG) gives the framework potentially broad applicability.

Empirical scope: The paper evaluates continuous image generation, autoregressive discrete image generation, and video generation. The reported improvements over the corresponding SFT models are substantial; for example, Xomni improves from 41.36 to 54.24 on UniGen, while Wan2.1 improves from 73.02 to 75.71 on the overall VBench score.

Analysis: The comparison of discriminator backbones and the long-horizon experiment exposing FAIL-PG collapse provide useful practical observations rather than reporting only favorable endpoint results.
The limitations section honestly acknowledges adversarial instability, sensitivity to design choices, limited data scale, and dependence on capabilities already present in the base model.
weaknesses: Soundness: FAIL-PD is described as an exact, low-variance, unbiased pathwise or deterministic-policy gradient, but the implemented update uses the one-step approximation in Eq. 2 rather than differentiation through the generated ODE trajectory. Local linearity is merely assumed, with no error bound or comparison against the claimed full-trajectory gradient. Consequently, the assertions that FAIL-PD is an 'unbiased limit of DDPG' and inherits GAN convergence properties are unsupported.

Soundness: The claimed imitation-learning interpretation is overstated. The discriminator matches terminal prompt-image distributions using expert images; there are no expert trajectories, actions, or state-action occupancy measures as in GAIL. The manuscript does not establish that this terminal conditional-GAN objective remedies behavioral-cloning covariate shift or compounding error.

Soundness: FAIL-PG substitutes differences of conditional-flow-matching losses for both log-likelihood ratios and KL divergence. Appendix A explicitly moves from an ELBO inequality to treating the ELBO as a tight proxy, but gives neither conditions nor empirical validation of tightness. Eq. 4 is therefore not generally a KL divergence and could even yield inappropriate per-sample estimates, undermining the PPO-style clipping and KL-constrained interpretation.

Evaluation: Results are reported without independent seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Given the known instability of adversarial training and the small differences among several methods, single-run endpoint scores do not support strong comparative conclusions.

Evaluation: The evidence for human-preference alignment consists only of learned automatic metrics, including HPSv3 and UnifiedReward; there is no human evaluation. The claim that FAIL solves reward hacking is especially too strong: Table 3 and eight selected examples show improvement on a few proxy metrics, but do not establish diversity preservation or robustness to discriminator/reward exploitation.

Evaluation: The training prompts include a subset of UniGen-Bench's train-en-short prompts, while evaluation is also stated to use en-short. The paper does not document a disjoint prompt split. Thus the prominent UniGen system comparison may measure prompt-level training overlap rather than generalization. Only DPG-Bench is identified as zero-shot.

Evaluation/presentation: Comparisons against frontier systems are difficult to interpret because those models differ in training data, model scale, sampling procedures, and likely resolution. The paper reports optimal CFG for its system-level checkpoints but does not establish a controlled common inference or evaluation protocol for all external baselines.

Reproducibility: The abstract says 'Code and data are available at' but supplies no URL. Important details remain absent, including seeds, parameter-efficient versus full-model tuning, sampling group size G, number of policy epochs E, clipping threshold, discriminator-warmup details outside the main image experiment, hybrid-loss weighting, timestep/step-size choices, checkpoint selection, and total compute. The proprietary Gemini-generated training data and API-based evaluator create additional reproducibility barriers.

Presentation: Several explanatory conclusions are speculative—for example, attributing stability to preservation of the flow manifold and discriminator robustness to reduced feature-space overfitting—without measurements of manifold preservation, diversity, or gradient behavior. Numerous grammatical errors and an incorrect citation of DPG-Bench to Silver et al. further reduce clarity and confidence.

Limitations/ethics: Although optimization limitations are discussed, the paper contains no meaningful treatment of data provenance, licensing and consent for web-scraped prompts or proprietary synthetic outputs, inherited generative-model biases, misuse risks, or the environmental cost of training across 32 H20 GPUs. These omissions are material for a generative-model post-training study.

strengths: Soundness: The core adversarial distribution-matching formulation is plausible, and the paper provides substantial empirical evidence across FLUX, Xomni, and Wan2.1. Comparisons with SFT, online DPO, and reward-based optimization consistently show meaningful gains on prompt-following and preference-model metrics.

Significance: Learning from 13,000 single-image demonstrations without explicit preference pairs is practically appealing. The improvements over FLUX.1-dev are sizable, and the demonstrated use of FAIL as a regularizer against reward hacking could be useful beyond the standalone method.

Originality: Casting generative-model post-training as adversarial imitation learning and developing complementary pathwise-gradient and flow-policy-gradient variants offers a coherent new perspective. Extension to both continuous and discrete generators strengthens the contribution.

The discriminator-backbone ablation, long-horizon comparison of FAIL-PD and FAIL-PG, and combined reward/FAIL experiments are informative. In particular, the observed rapid collapse of FAIL-PG versus continued improvement of FAIL-PD gives practitioners useful guidance.

Presentation is generally well organized, with clear algorithms, extensive quantitative tables, qualitative examples, and an honest limitations section acknowledging adversarial instability, uncertain scaling, and dependence on pretrained capabilities.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several theoretical claims are stronger than their support. FAIL-PD is described as computing an exact pathwise gradient and as an unbiased limit of DDPG, yet the implemented update uses a single-step denoising approximation whose bias is neither characterized nor empirically isolated. The claimed inherited local convergence properties of GANs are also not established.

The FAIL-PG likelihood ratio and KL penalty replace log likelihoods with differences of conditional flow-matching losses through an ELBO proxy. The appendix acknowledges this approximation but does not justify when the bound is sufficiently tight; consequently, the resulting quantity need not behave like an actual per-sample likelihood ratio or nonnegative KL divergence.

Equation 2 becomes ill-conditioned as t+Δt approaches 1, while t is stated to be sampled uniformly on [0,1]. The manuscript does not specify endpoint truncation or another numerical safeguard. Important implementation details such as the exact timestep distribution, Δt, sampling schedules, policy parameterization, and hyperparameter-selection protocol are missing.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on learned automatic evaluators, with no blinded human study, uncertainty intervals, multiple-seed results, or significance tests. This is particularly limiting for claims about human preference, aesthetics, diversity preservation, and elimination of reward hacking. Using a Gemini-based evaluator for system-level UniGen evaluation when expert images also come from Gemini creates a potential ecosystem bias that is not analyzed.

Some headline reporting is inconsistent: the introduction says FAIL raises the FLUX baseline from 61.61 to 73.70, whereas Table 7 reports FLUX.1-dev at 61.30 and assigns 61.61 to Janus-Pro. The different ablation and system-level evaluators also produce substantially different scores and should be signposted more clearly. DPG-Bench is repeatedly cited to the deterministic policy-gradient paper, indicating citation-quality issues.

Originality relative to recent adversarial-reward image-generation work is not sharply established. The paper discusses GAN-based diffusion training and cites a highly related adversarial-reward approach, but does not provide a direct conceptual or empirical comparison sufficient to isolate what is new beyond adapting adversarial distribution matching to flow-model optimization.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract's code/data link is blank, and the paper omits seeds, variance, complete training schedules, checkpoint-selection rules, dataset filtering criteria, baseline tuning budgets, and enough architectural detail to reconstruct all variants. Reliance on 32 H20 GPUs and proprietary Gemini-generated expert data further raises the replication barrier.

The limitations discussion is welcome but does not cover research ethics: dataset and model licensing, provenance and permitted use of synthetic expert images, inherited demographic or cultural biases, possible unsafe generation, and misuse risks are absent. These are not necessarily fatal, but should be addressed for a generative-image system.

strengths: Significance: The problem is relevant: improving generative-model post-training without separately collected preference pairs could be useful, and the discriminator-as-regularizer results suggest a potentially valuable direction for limiting reward overoptimization.

Empirical breadth: The paper evaluates continuous image generation, discrete-token image generation, and video generation, and includes comparisons with SFT, online DPO, and reward-based optimization as well as discriminator, data-scale, initialization, and compute ablations.

The reported improvements over the authors' SFT checkpoints are substantial on several automated metrics; the distribution-distance analysis and long-horizon curves also provide useful evidence beyond a single endpoint.

Presentation: The high-level distinction between pathwise discriminator gradients (FAIL-PD) and scalar-reward updates (FAIL-PG) is easy to understand, and the algorithms and qualitative samples communicate the intended workflow.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript candidly notes adversarial instability, dependence on initialization and base-model capabilities, uncertain scaling, inherited expert-data biases, and misuse risks such as deepfakes.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central theoretical characterization is not established. Equation 1 is a GAN objective over generated samples, but FAIL-PD does not differentiate that objective through the full sampler: it detaches a completed rollout, re-noises it, and differentiates a one-step reconstruction surrogate. Consequently, claims that it computes an exact pathwise gradient, is an unbiased limit of DDPG, inherits GAN convergence, or minimizes the stated policy-expert Jensen-Shannon divergence are unsupported. The reconstruction PSNR/LPIPS experiment only measures local reconstruction error and does not validate gradient bias or objective equivalence.

The FAIL-PD update is underspecified and potentially ill-defined near the endpoint: t is sampled uniformly on [0,1], while Equation 2 divides by 1-(t+Delta t), which becomes singular at t+Delta t=1 and changes sign beyond it. No timestep truncation or boundary handling is reported.

FAIL-PG also rests on a consequential approximation presented too strongly. A conditional-flow-matching ELBO is not generally the exact sample log likelihood, so exponentiating differences of CFM losses is not a valid importance ratio without additional assumptions. Likewise, the difference of two ELBO proxies is not necessarily KL(pi_theta||pi_ref) and need not even be nonnegative. Thus the claimed PPO/KL interpretation and resulting policy-gradient justification require theory or direct validation.

The imitation-learning framing is incomplete for conditional generation. The main objective is written for marginal image distributions and omits prompts or state-action occupancy measures. It is therefore unclear precisely what distribution is matched and in what sense the method solves the distribution-shift problem associated with behavioral cloning.

Evaluation evidence is insufficient for the breadth of the claims. Results use only automated evaluators, with no human preference study, independent replication seeds, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests. The discrete-image and video extensions each receive essentially one base/SFT comparison, so they do not establish a general-purpose method relative to relevant post-training alternatives.

Several comparisons are difficult to interpret fairly. Methods use different training horizons; the reward model is deliberately trained from only the same 13K demonstrations; Online DPO always labels the expert as preferred; and system-level comparisons mix externally reported frontier models with the authors' 512x512, tuned-CFG generations. FLUX scores also vary sharply across tables (for example, UniGen 51.84 versus about 61 and DPG 76.74 versus 83.84), without an adequately controlled reconciliation.

There is a possible benchmark-contamination issue: training prompts are drawn partly from UniGen-Bench's train-en-short split, while evaluation is described as using en-short. Exact prompt splits and overlap checks are not provided. DPG offers some zero-shot evidence, but this ambiguity materially weakens the headline UniGen result.

Originality is moderate rather than high. GAN-style adversarial training for diffusion/flow models is well established, and the two optimization routes largely combine a standard pathwise discriminator loss with the existing FPO surrogate. The paper does not sharply distinguish its technical contribution from prior adversarial diffusion training and distillation beyond relabeling the setup as imitation learning.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance. The abstract says code and data are available but gives no URL. Important details are missing or unclear, including the exact released prompt/image set and filtering procedure, SFT recipe, Delta t and endpoint treatment, update ratios, loss weights, PPO clipping and epoch settings, sampling/evaluation seeds, and complete system-comparison protocols. Training also requires 32 H20 GPUs.

Presentation needs substantial editing: there are numerous grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology and baseline numbers, an unresolved 'Figure ??' reference, mismatched figure numbering, questionable citations such as DPG-Bench being attributed to the deterministic-policy-gradient paper, and claims such as 'solving' reward hacking that overreach the reported metric-based evidence.

strengths: The core practical idea—using an online discriminator to align flow-model outputs with expert demonstrations—is potentially useful, and the paper provides both a differentiable pathwise variant and an FPO-based policy-gradient variant.

The empirical study is broad: it examines discriminator architectures, training dynamics, expert-data scale, cold-start initialization, wall-clock cost, feature-space distribution distances, reward-model integration, and extensions to discrete image and video generation.

Reported improvements over SFT are substantial on several automated benchmarks. In particular, the reward-plus-FAIL results suggest that dynamic distribution matching may help regularize optimization against a fixed reward model.

The manuscript explicitly acknowledges adversarial instability, dependence on the pretrained model, limited scaling evidence, inherited expert-data biases, and possible misuse. These are appropriate limitations rather than reasons for additional penalty.
weaknesses: Soundness: the claimed equivalence to imitation learning is not established. Equation 1 is an endpoint conditional GAN objective, whereas classical adversarial imitation learning matches state-action occupancy measures. The paper neither defines the relevant flow-policy occupancy distribution nor proves that its procedure addresses the sequential covariate-shift argument used to motivate the work.

Soundness: FAIL-PD is repeatedly described as an exact, low-variance, unbiased policy gradient, but the implemented update uses a local one-step denoising approximation rather than differentiation through the complete ODE trajectory. Equation 2 is also ill-conditioned as t+Delta t approaches 1, while the algorithm samples t uniformly over [0,1] without specifying boundary handling. Appendix B measures reconstruction quality on synthetic noised model outputs, not gradient bias or agreement with full-trajectory differentiation, so it does not validate the central optimization claim.

Soundness: the FAIL-PG likelihood ratio and KL regularizer are not rigorously justified. An ELBO lower bound does not imply that differences of CFM losses equal differences of true log likelihoods; approximation gaps need not cancel between two models. Consequently, Equations 3–4 need not yield a valid density ratio or nonnegative KL divergence, also weakening the interpretation of the per-sample 'KL' masking method.

Evaluation validity: expert-data prompts are drawn partly from UniGen-Bench's train-en-short split, and Appendix D evaluates on that same named split. This creates apparent train/test overlap while the paper advertises zero-shot generalization. A clearly disjoint prompt split and leakage analysis are essential, especially because the qualitative trajectories closely approach individual expert references.

The evidence lacks uncertainty estimates, independent training seeds, human evaluation, and diversity or memorization analysis. Nearly all conclusions—including 'human preference alignment,' monotonic improvement, and prevention of reward hacking—rest on automated reward/evaluator models. Selected qualitative examples cannot establish these claims, and no prompts or selection protocol are given.

Baseline support is inadequate. Online DPO is implemented by always declaring the single expert image preferable to every policy sample, and the RLHF reward model is trained from similarly constructed pairs; these are unusually restrictive baselines. There is no controlled comparison with strong existing adversarial diffusion/distillation or distribution-matching methods, and standalone FPO is only presented in a separate reward-integration experiment.

The discrete-image and video generalization claims each rely on one model and one aggregate table, without strong task-specific preference-optimization baselines, repeated runs, or qualitative failure analysis. This is insufficient evidence for the claimed general-purpose or universal applicability.

Originality is limited relative to the claims: the principal objective is a standard GAN loss over expert and generated endpoints, FAIL-PG largely combines a GAIL-style discriminator with existing FPO, and FAIL-PD resembles differentiable reward/adversarial fine-tuning with a one-step approximation. The related-work discussion does not sharply distinguish the contribution from adversarial diffusion training, distribution-matching distillation, or the cited contemporaneous adversarial-reward approach.

Reproducibility is poor. The abstract says code and data are available but the rendered manuscript contains no URL. Important details are missing, including Delta t and timestep boundary handling, PPO clipping and epoch settings, group size, discriminator/policy update ratios, SFT cold-start recipe, checkpoint-selection procedure, seeds, and tuning protocol. Reproduction additionally depends on proprietary Gemini expert generations and Gemini-based evaluation plus 32 H20 GPUs.

Presentation has numerous correctness and polish problems: inconsistent baseline scores across tables are only indirectly attributable to different evaluators/CFG settings; DPG-Bench is incorrectly cited to the deterministic policy-gradient paper; references are duplicated; Figure '??' remains unresolved; figure numbering is inconsistent; and frequent grammatical errors impede precise interpretation.

Significance and ethics are overstated. The method may be useful if validated, but 13,000 proprietary expert generations and large-scale GPU training do not establish 'democratized' alignment, and the evidence shows mitigation rather than a solution to reward hacking. Although the impact statement discusses bias and deepfakes, it omits data provenance, licensing or consent for web-sourced prompts/images, proprietary-teacher distillation concerns, memorization risk, and concrete safety evaluation.

strengths: Significance: The paper targets an important practical problem—post-training large flow-matching generators from demonstrations without a separately trained static reward model—and reports meaningful gains over FLUX.1-dev. For example, FAIL-PD improves the system-level UniGen score from 61.30 to 73.70 and DPG from 83.84 to 87.32 (Tables 6–7).

Soundness/empirical breadth: The evaluation is unusually broad, covering two optimization variants, three discriminator backbones, continuous and discrete image generation, video generation, reward-model integration, training dynamics, expert-data scaling, cold-start dependence, wall-clock cost, and feature-space distribution distances.

The results expose useful practical behavior rather than presenting only favorable endpoints: FAIL-PG converges rapidly but can collapse, whereas FAIL-PD improves more slowly and remains stable through 2,000 steps. The cold-start and KL-masking ablations further clarify when the methods work.

Originality: Combining an online adversarial discriminator with flow-model pathwise and policy-gradient updates is a useful synthesis. The one-step FAIL-PD construction and the application of discriminator rewards through FPO offer potentially valuable recipes even though the overarching objective resembles established GAN training.

Presentation: The main algorithmic distinction is easy to follow, tables and qualitative examples are extensive, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges adversarial instability, uncertain scaling, and dependence on pretrained capabilities.
Ethics: The impact statement appropriately identifies replication of harmful expert-data biases and misuse for deepfakes or misinformation, and recommends expert-data vetting and safety filtering.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several central theoretical claims are overstated. The manuscript does not establish that generative post-training is “mathematically equivalent” to imitation learning; Eq. 1 is endpoint GAN distribution matching rather than state-action occupancy matching. Likewise, FAIL-PD is called an “exact,” “unbiased limit of DDPG,” although the implemented update uses the explicitly approximate one-step reconstruction in Eq. 2. No theorem or bias analysis supports these assertions.

The purported KL in Eq. 4 is only a proxy. Subtracting two negative-ELBO/CFM losses does not generally yield a log-likelihood ratio because the ELBO gaps can be model-dependent; consequently, the expression is not guaranteed to be a nonnegative KL divergence. Appendix A cancels a shared constant but does not address these unequal gaps. The same concern affects the FPO likelihood-ratio approximation in Eq. 3.

The one-step approximation study in Table 9 measures reconstruction fidelity of samples produced by the current model, but does not show that the resulting policy gradient approximates the full-solver gradient. Gradient cosine similarity, bias, downstream comparison with full unrolling, and sensitivity to timestep or step size are missing.

Evaluation relies entirely on learned automatic judges, including HPSv3, UnifiedReward, Qwen-72B, and Gemini 2.5 Pro. There is no blinded human evaluation despite repeated claims about human-preference alignment, aesthetics, semantic fidelity, and parity with frontier systems. No confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported, so relatively small differences such as FAIL-PG versus Online DPO are difficult to interpret.

Potential benchmark contamination is insufficiently resolved: training prompts are drawn partly from a UniGen “train-en-short” split, while evaluation is described as using the UniGen “en-short” split. The manuscript should explicitly demonstrate prompt and semantic deduplication. The independently evaluated DPG results help, but do not resolve the reported UniGen gains.

Originality is not positioned convincingly against the closest prior art. The method’s basic objective is standard conditional GAN training on expert and policy endpoints, and the paper does not experimentally compare against adversarial diffusion objectives or clearly distinguish itself from the cited “Image as Its Own Reward: Reinforcement Learning with Adversarial Reward for Image Generation.” Calling the method imitation learning does not by itself establish a new technical principle.

Baseline fairness and implementation are not fully documented. It is unclear whether Online DPO and RLHF receive the identical SFT cold start, hyperparameter-search budget, and compute budget; SFT training details are also absent. FAIL-PD at 800 or 2,000 steps is compared narratively with several 400-step baselines, while Table 14 reports per-step rather than total training cost.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate for a large-scale empirical paper. The abstract says code and data are available “at” but gives no link. Random seeds, sampling seeds, scheduler and optimizer details beyond learning rates, LoRA/full-finetuning choices, discriminator-update ratios, loss weights, timestep sampling details, SFT configuration, and complete system-level CFG settings are missing. Reproduction also requires 32 H20 GPUs and proprietary Gemini-generated expert data/judging.

Presentation has several consequential errors: DPG-Bench is incorrectly cited to the deterministic policy-gradient paper; CLIP is cited to the SHAP paper; the text reports the FLUX UniGen baseline as 61.61 although Table 7 lists 61.30; and Appendix G contains an unresolved “Figure ??” reference. These mistakes reduce confidence in the evaluation audit trail.

The limitations and ethics discussions are welcome but omit important issues raised by the actual setup: licensing/provenance and possible memorization of proprietary expert outputs, benchmark leakage, dependence on proprietary evaluators, demographic bias measurement, and the substantial computational cost of repeated online rollouts. Overall, the empirical promise is clear, but the theoretical overclaims and reproducibility/evaluation gaps require substantial revision before the conclusions are reliable enough for acceptance.
